approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would create a national system to reduce harm from waste and products.
It would ban exporting unprocessed waste glass, plastics, tyres and paper unless they are turned into reusable materials.
The bill would replace the Product Stewardship Act 2011 and let the Minister make rules that are subject to parliamentary oversight.
Establishes a framework to regulate waste exports and product stewardship.
Bans the export of untreated waste glass, plastics, tyres and paper.
Repeals the Product Stewardship Act 2011 and replaces it with new rules.
Sets obligations for businesses involved in making, importing, distributing or designing certain products.
Provides enforcement powers including licence suspension, civil penalties and criminal offences.
Allows fees on a cost-recovery basis for Commonwealth activities under the bill.
Manufacturers, importers, distributors, designers, exporters, businesses, community organisations and individuals involved in waste exports and product stewardship schemes.

To read a bill a [second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/) is to agree with its main idea. The Recycling and Waste Reduction (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2020 repeals the Product Stewardship Act 2011 and transitions its provisions into the new Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, ensuring continuity for existing schemes like the National Television and Computer Recycling Scheme without disruption to industry or the public.

The Recycling and Waste Reduction Charges (General) Bill 2020 enables cost recovery for administering the waste export ban, which phases out exports of waste glass from 1 January 2021, mixed plastics from 1 July 2021, whole used tyres from 1 December 2021, single polymer plastics from 1 July 2022, and mixed paper and cardboard from 1 July 2024.

The government introduced the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 to phase out the export of 645,000 tonnes of unprocessed plastic, paper, glass and tyres, aiming to create over 10,000 jobs and divert over 10 million tonnes from landfill, backed by a $190 million Recycling Modernisation Fund.

Labor supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 but moved an amendment criticising the government's chronic delay and poor handling of waste reform, noting that only 12% of Australia's 100kg per capita plastic waste is recycled, $120 million of a $167 million recycling package remained unspent after 18 months, and the 70% plastic packaging recycling target for 2025 is far off track at 16%.

Labor supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 but argued it was a missed opportunity, noting Australia recycles only 12% of plastics and 58% of total waste, and that the government allocated just $10 million in the budget for growing waste and recycling capacity.

The speaker argued in support of the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, which will ban waste exports, divert 10 million tonnes of waste from landfill, generate an extra $1.5 billion in the economy and create hundreds of jobs over 20 years. Specific timelines include bans on unprocessed mixed plastics by 1 July 2021, whole used tyres by December 2021, single resin plastics by July 2022, and mixed paper/cardboard by July 2024.

The speaker supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, arguing Australia generates 67 million tonnes of waste annually but recycles only 37 million, with just 12% of plastic waste recycled. The bill aims to end the export of 640,000 tonnes of rubbish and establish a national recycling framework, backed by a $190 million Recycling Modernisation Fund and a $60 million National Waste Policy Action Plan to create 10,000 jobs.

Labor supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, arguing the Coalition wasted seven years on waste policy and that the $100 million Recycling Investment Fund was a repackaged existing fund. The opposition committed to a $20 billion Rewiring the Nation plan, net zero emissions by 2050, and increasing Australia's plastics recycling capacity by 400%.

The Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 bans waste exports in phases from July 2021, establishes product stewardship schemes, and aims to generate $1.5 billion in economic activity and 10,000 jobs through a $191 million Recycling Modernisation Fund.

The Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 bans the export of unprocessed waste glass, plastic, tyres and paper, improves product stewardship, and is projected to create 10,000 jobs over 10 years. The speaker highlighted local businesses Licella and iQRenew as examples of innovation in waste recycling.

Support was expressed for the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, highlighting South Australia’s container deposit legislation since 1977 and plastic bag ban since 2009. A proposed recycling hub in McLaren Vale from three councils was noted, projected to create over 80 construction and 20 ongoing jobs, with encouragement for federal and state support.

The Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 bans waste exports (mixed plastics from July 2021, whole tyres from December 2021, single plastics from 2022, paper and cardboard from July 2024) and strengthens product stewardship through voluntary, co-regulatory and mandatory schemes, with additional investments like the Recycling Modernisation Fund.

The speaker argued that Australia's recycling performance has declined, with only 9.4% of 3.4 million tonnes of plastic recycled in 2017-18, and criticised the government for seven years of inaction on product stewardship. They highlighted the Bower's right-to-repair campaign and called for community-led recycling initiatives in Parramatta, noting that the major recycling contract expires in two years.

The speaker argued that the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 embodies Liberal principles of stewardship, aiming to reduce waste, promote a circular economy, and create economic opportunities. He praised Assistant Minister for Waste Reduction and Environmental Management Trevor Evans for advancing practical, industry-inclusive reforms to improve environmental outcomes and build a sustainable 21st-century economy.

The speaker argued that the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 is a positive step but does not go far enough, citing Australia’s 12% plastic recycling rate and the government’s failure to invest in product stewardship funds. They highlighted that 4,000 microplastic pieces per square metre are found on Sydney beaches, 14 million tonnes of plastic sit on the ocean floor, and Australia’s export ban by 2024 requires a 400% increase in domestic reprocessing capacity.

The speaker supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, which introduces a sequential ban on exporting unprocessed waste including plastic, paper, glass, and tyres. The bill aims to reduce waste by 10% per person by 2030, recover 80% of waste, increase recycled content use, and phase out problematic plastics by 2025, with $190 million allocated for recycling modernisation.

The speaker supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, citing that 76% of Warringah residents listed waste as their top issue and noting Australia uses 130 kg of plastic per person annually with only 9% recycled. They called for stronger measures including packaging content targets, a ban on single-use plastics, and five-yearly reviews, while commending the government’s $250 million Recycling Modernisation Fund and $1.5 billion Manufacturing Strategy.

The Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 was supported but criticised as too little too late, with the Morrison government accused of failing to deliver on promised recycling infrastructure; Australia generated 67 million tonnes of waste in 2016-17 and recycles only 12% of plastic, while local initiatives like the City of Newcastle's $24 million organics recycling facility and Feedback Organic Recovery's 700,000 litre food waste diversion were highlighted.

The speaker argued that the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 and related bills will create a recycling industry in Australia, with $190 million in infrastructure funding expected to generate 10,000 jobs and eliminate 10 million tonnes of landfill, while banning waste exports to guarantee supply for domestic recyclers. They highlighted the need for cost-effective regional recycling capacity, citing South Australia's long-running container deposit scheme and the potential for e-waste processing at Port Pirie's smelter.

The MP for Dunkley argued the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill is insufficient, noting that while Labor will support it, the government still lags behind the environmental action of young people in schools like Frankston High School and Elisabeth Murdoch College. They cited community suggestions for tax offsets for businesses reducing waste, government‑owned recycling plants, and a shift away from single‑use plastics.

The speaker supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, arguing it establishes a national framework for waste management and an export ban on waste plastic, paper, glass, and tyres, expected to generate $1.5 billion in economic activity over 20 years. They cited specific local recycling initiatives in the electorate of Forde, including grants to Beenleigh and Marsden State High Schools, and named companies like Gold Coast Resource Recovery, V Resource, Molectra, Recycling Developments, BlockTexx, and TES.

Labor supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020 and its export ban on waste, but criticised the government for taking credit for a ban forced by China and other countries' import restrictions, noting Australia now has less recycling infrastructure than in 2005 and produces 100 kilograms of plastic waste per capita annually.

The speaker supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill 2020, highlighting South Australia’s leadership in recycling since the 1970s and criticising the federal government for seven years of inaction, including a $100 million recycling fund that remains untouched. Concrete figures cited include Australia recycling only 12% of plastics and 58% of total waste, with a need to increase local plastic reprocessing capacity by 400%.

The speaker supported the Recycling and Waste Reduction Bill, citing local initiatives like Envorinex (which received over $700,000 in federal funding, doubling its workforce and processing 500 kg of soft plastics per hour) and the ASPIRE digital waste platform. The bill ends the export of 645,000 tonnes of waste annually, invests $1 billion to create 10,000 jobs, and aims to divert 10 million tonnes from landfill.
